question:
A set of three points is chosen randomly from the grid shown. Each three-point set has the same probability of being chosen. What is the probability that the points lie on the same straight line?

[Figure 1](figures/2004_AMC_10A_Q05_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
Since every three-point set is equally likely, we can count all sets and then count those lying on a straight line. The grid has \(3\times3=9\) points, so the total number of sets is
\[
\binom{9}{3}=\frac{9\cdot8\cdot7}{3\cdot2\cdot1}=84.
\]
The division removes the six possible orders of each set of three points.

There are three horizontal triples, one in each row. Any nonhorizontal line contains at most one point from each row, so a nonhorizontal collinear triple must use all three rows. Because the rows are equally spaced, the middle-row point must be horizontally halfway between the top-row and bottom-row points.

If those two endpoints are in the same column, this gives one of the three vertical triples. If they are in different columns, their horizontal midpoint is a grid point only when they occupy the two outer columns. These give the two corner-to-corner diagonals. Endpoints in neighboring columns would have their midpoint between columns.

Thus there are exactly \(3+3+2=8\) favorable sets. Each listed line contains exactly three grid points, and distinct lines cannot contain the same triple. Therefore the probability is
\[
\frac{8}{84}=\boxed{\frac{2}{21}},
\]
which is choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
